g.passage: When the last crate of my father's records was sold, Ofelia counted the bills twice on the folding table between the lemons and the fish stalls of the Valparaiso market. I had called her Señora all morning, the way I called the woman who ran the bakery, and she answered to it without correcting me. The plan had been hers: sell the records before the rent came due, keep the apartment, keep me at the same school. It had worked. A man in a striped scarf carried off the jazz albums, and a student took the rest in two trips. Ofelia divided the bills into two stacks, slid the thicker one toward me, and said, Count it, Emiliano. She folded the thinner one into her apron. Then, while I was watching the gulls over the harbor, she took the thinner stack out again, set it on top of mine, and smoothed the empty apron pocket flat. Neither of us mentioned it. On the walk uphill she carried the empty crates.

g.passage: Who keeps a radio playing through a wall for eleven years without once asking whether anyone minds? I did, on the old barge moored below the Busan fish wharf, where my cabin and Bokhee's share a single plank partition and my name, Eunseo, is painted on the door in white. I have always called her Mrs. Bokhee and bowed at the gangway, and she has always bowed back, a little lower. Each New Year she left a jar of pickled radish outside my door; I left nothing, assuming the radish was simply what neighbors on the river did. This spring I switched the radio off at nine and kept it off. On the third quiet night I heard her drag something heavy across her floor. In the morning, through her open door, I saw her narrow bed pushed back against our shared wall, its old place by the drafty window now empty, a square of unfaded boards showing where it had stood for years. I bought radish seeds that afternoon.

Somewhere past Giza she took it down and began on the stack in her lap, circling, striking, writing a small hard number at the top of each page. When the door slid open, Yusuf stood there with a ticket for the same compartment. He had been her student four years earlier; she had once written a single red word across his final essay, and he had left the course the next week. He sat across from her. Neither spoke. She went on grading, and now the pencil hovered above each margin before it touched, and twice she lifted it without making a mark. Yusuf took a notebook from his bag and wrote, page after page. g.passage: Four rules held in the tailor's back room, which Weiqi and I rented on alternating mornings in that Vermont winter to proof our dough: no talk of prices, no borrowing flour, no opening the window, and nothing of mine crosses the chalk line on the floor. I had drawn that line myself, heel to heel across the boards, and each Monday I traced it again so it would not wear away. Weiqi, whose bakery stood three doors from mine, kept to her side without comment. On Thursday a letter arrived with the tailor's name on it, and Weiqi, thinking it was for her, had opened it before she noticed. It was from the landlord: the building would be sold in spring. She read it aloud to me anyway, standing on her side. We stood a long while among the rising bowls. When she left, I stepped forward, and my boot rested on the chalk. My name is Matheus, and I did not retrace it that Monday, or the next.

g.passage: Polishing the brass bell was the first chore Kai ever gave Tallulah, in 1921, after the galley of a scrapped steamer was hauled by rail to Albuquerque and bolted down as a lunch counter on Central Avenue. The counter had come to the two of them jointly from Kai's brother, and by the fourth summer Tallulah wanted to sell her half and ride west. Kai heard her out over the evening dishes. For a week after, orders went up by voice alone; the bell hung dull and silent, and no one touched the rag folded beside it. Tara's aunt set down rice pudding for Eid. Hari, who had sailed cargo ships for thirty years and now lived above the shop, arrived with a brass plate of marigolds and sweets for his evening prayer. Three times he set the plate down near the corner, and three times he drew it back toward his chest when someone reached past him. Hari's plate rode at the table's rim, an anchored skiff off a crowded quay. Tara shifted the pudding bowls to open a gap. He looked at the gap and kept still, holding the plate level. g.passage: Years later I still picture Angus at the crossing below Kelvin Mill, where the burn had dried that August to a bed of grey stones. I was nineteen and clerked for him three mornings a week, long after he had left the bench; he called me Miss Maeve and never anything shorter. Every morning he carried an envelope addressed in his own hand to a man he had once sentenced, and every morning, at the near edge of the stones, he pressed two fingers flat against the pocket that held it. For him that envelope was a ford walked daily toward a bank that never came nearer. I would wait with the satchel while he stood there. On the last dry morning, with not a trickle left between the stones, he stepped out to the middle, stood beside a flat rock as long as it takes to read a page, and walked back to me. We went round by the bridge.

lifting what the wind brought down,

g.passage: Eulalio set the copper pot on the boarding-house stove each evening and made you repeat the farewells until the beans went soft. In the valley, he told you, a guest does not simply leave; the leaving has an order, and he drilled you in it, correcting the place of each word, the pause before the blessing, the second thanks for the salt. For six weeks, Anacleto, you practiced while the landlady shelled peas by the window. On the morning your coach left for Puebla, you stood at the kitchen door with your bag, ready to recite the whole of it to him. His own farewell was ______. He touched two fingers to your sleeve, said a single word, and turned back to stir the pot before you could begin.

g.passage:
Nobody comes in the rains.
The Regal on Galle Road shows its one film to empty rows,
and every night at nine Ruwan climbs to the booth,
threads the reel, and runs it through for no one,
as he has each monsoon since the clinic moved upstairs.
This year the water reached the second step.
Mehreen came in her council sash with the last boat ticket
folded in her palm and held it out to him under the screen light.
His answer was ______.
He opened his black umbrella, closed her fingers around its handle,
and walked down to the third row, where the leak was worst,
to set a bucket under it before the second reel.

g.passage: Aluva station, at the far end of the Kochi metro line, was empty at six except for you, Priya, and Vikram with a cardboard box. For eleven years of rehearsals he had wound the brass metronome himself before every session, and if a cellist reached for it, he moved it a few inches away without breaking his sentence. His mother's house in Kakkanad had been emptied that week; the piano was sold, the shelves taken apart, and the box held the last thing left. He took out the metronome and gave it to you, the youngest of the second violins, in a manner that was ______. g.passage: Three tasks filled each morning in the glasshouses outside Gdansk in the spring of 1913: the daughter brought her mother warm tea from the third row, the leaf the old woman swore tasted of Darjeeling; she logged the overnight temperature in the green ledger; and she carried a letter to Pavel in the cottage by the boiler. The letters were long and full of news. She described the new shoots, the cook's quarrel with the coal man, the mild weather promised for May, and the doctor's opinion, which in her pages grew more hopeful each week. She read them aloud to him because his eyes had failed. That Thursday she read slowly. She stopped after the weather. She sat. Through the glass the rows went on. Pavel's hand already lay on the blank side of yesterday's page, which he had turned face down on the blanket before she came in.
